issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette:
Linda is a 72-year-old North American woman who has worked for years as a network engineer, a role that still structures much of her week around office visits, server rooms, and occasional trips across the city. She is married and describes herself as someone who had always taken pride in being steady, practical, and able to keep her focus in busy environments. That changed after she witnessed a traumatic incident on a city bus. She had been riding home on a crowded afternoon route, standing in the aisle with other passengers packed close, half listening to a conversation nearby, when a violent event unfolded in front of her. In the confusion of bodies, raised voices, and people trying to move at once, she saw another person seriously harmed. What has stayed with her is not only the shock of seeing it happen, but the helplessness of being trapped in the crowd and unable to get away from the scene.

In the days afterward, Linda found that ordinary parts of city life had become charged. Crowded places, especially shopping centers or public events, no longer felt like routine inconveniences. They felt dangerous. If she entered a busy store and saw people bunching together in an aisle, she immediately began scanning who was standing where, how close the exits were, and whether anyone’s tone of voice sounded tense. She had come to believe she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Bus riding became particularly potent. Even seeing a bus pull up could make her body tighten. If she had to think about taking one, what came to mind was the press of strangers, the inability to move freely, and the sense that disaster could break out without warning.

Certain conversation topics also became difficult in ways that embarrassed her. If coworkers at the office started discussing assaults on the news, public safety, or incidents on transit, Linda would go quiet or leave the break area altogether. In meetings she remained capable and precise, but casual conversation had become another place where she felt on guard. She noticed that other people could talk about upsetting events and then move on, while she felt abruptly set apart from them. Over time she began to think of herself as permanently an outsider now, someone who had seen something other people had not and could not really understand.

Over the months, Linda developed habits that made sense to her as ways of getting through the day. She avoided the site of the event entirely, changing her route across the city even when it made errands or work trips longer. She stopped taking buses and arranged her schedule around driving or asking her husband for rides. When her office hosted gatherings downtown, she often declined if she expected packed rooms or street congestion. At home and at work she tried to manage herself by forcing only positive thoughts. If her mind drifted toward what she had witnessed or toward the idea that crowds were unsafe, she would quickly tell herself to look on the bright side, to be grateful, to think about pleasant things instead. She described this almost as a discipline: if she stayed positive enough, maybe she could keep herself composed. Yet the effort left her strained. Her husband noticed that she sounded flat when he asked how she was doing, and she often brushed him off with reassuring phrases that did not match how tense she looked.

The consequences accumulated quietly. Linda became less willing to join her husband for concerts, festivals, or busy restaurants. Shopping trips were cut short or postponed. Even professionally, her world narrowed. As a network engineer, she sometimes needed to travel to busy office campuses or use shared transit routes for city-based appointments, and she increasingly organized tasks to avoid those settings. Colleagues saw her as more reserved than before, and Linda felt that reserve hardening into distance. The more she monitored the environment, the more convinced she became that the world is a dangerous place and that other people moved through it with a confidence she no longer had.

She sought help only after a recent workday when a crowded lobby and an overheard conversation about violence on public transportation left her so shaken that she abandoned the visit and waited outside for her husband to pick her up. What frightened her most was not just that crowded places and buses still affected her, but that this had become her life years later: detours, vigilance, and the sense of standing apart. She comes to treatment hoping she might regain some freedom to move through the city and be with other people again, while fearing that the danger she now sees everywhere may be the only realistic way to live.
